articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License, Issues New FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026.

This action modifies existing authorizations related to transactions involving Venezuela, underscoring OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions policy in response to ongoing developments in the region. The specific details of the amendments and the new FAQ provide updated guidance for entities engaging in or considering transactions with Venezuela.

The issuance reflects a continued effort by OFAC to fine-tune its sanctions programs, aiming to balance pressure on the Venezuelan regime with humanitarian considerations and targeted economic activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and Individuals, Sanctions Cuban Bank, Issues New GLs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a new round of Iran-related designations on October 15, 2026, targeting 16 individuals and 11 entities, adding them to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. These designations include financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies, aiming to further disrupt Iran's access to the global financial system.

In a related action, OFAC also designated Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, which has been under sanctions since 2020. This move highlights the U.S. government's concern over Cuba's role as an alleged outpost for malign actors and terror groups, including Iran.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs), providing updated guidance for authorized transactions. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez criticized the action as 'aggressive,' asserting BICSA is a legitimate bank with legitimate transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026.

This action indicates a targeted adjustment to the existing sanctions regime against Venezuela, potentially reflecting changes in the behavior of the designated entity or individual, or broader policy considerations.

Such removals are part of OFAC's ongoing review and recalibration of its sanctions lists, which can occur when designated parties meet specific criteria for delisting or when U.S. foreign policy objectives shift.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These designations aim to disrupt illicit financial networks that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to combating these threats.
The action underscores the U.S. government's strategy of using financial sanctions to isolate and incapacitate those who pose a threat to national security and international stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026.

This GL provides specific authorizations for certain transactions involving Russia, indicating a potential carve-out or clarification within the broader Russia sanctions program. Such licenses are often issued to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain journalistic activities, or other specific types of transactions deemed permissible under U.S. policy.
The issuance of this GL reflects OFAC's ongoing efforts to manage the scope and impact of its sanctions, ensuring they are precisely targeted while minimizing unintended consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License (GL) and an amended Russia-related General License.

These actions demonstrate OFAC's continued focus on countering Iran's destabilizing activities through financial pressure, while also adjusting its approach to Russia sanctions. The new Iran-related GL may provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, potentially related to humanitarian efforts or other limited engagements.

The amendment to the Russia-related GL suggests a recalibration of existing authorizations, reflecting the evolving geopolitical landscape and the U.S. government's ongoing assessment of its sanctions policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ, Removes Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 5, 2026, warning foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that they could be targeted without advance notification for transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

This alert, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aims to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime and follows a series of sanctions in September 2026. The amended FAQ 156 removes previous language suggesting OFAC would generally contact FFIs before making a finding of sanctionable activity, indicating a more aggressive enforcement stance.

Additionally, OFAC announced designations removals and updates, which could signify a streamlining of its sanctions lists or a response to changes in the status of previously designated entities or individuals.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026.
These designations target individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist activities, aiming to disrupt their financial networks and limit their ability to operate globally.
This action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to combating terrorism through financial sanctions, isolating those who facilitate or engage in acts of terror.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses Record $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a record $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for widespread violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. The bank's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to large numbers of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance and did not complete many significant steps needed to establish an effective program. This penalty is the largest in OCC history and underscores the agency's commitment to enforcing BSA/AML compliance.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank and its parent and affiliated entities on October 8, 2026.
This action addresses significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money-Laundering (AML) compliance, along with enterprise-wide financial crimes compliance programs.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training, with its risk assessment failing to sufficiently address the risks associated with its credit and charge-card business.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced the addition of more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. These entities, primarily from China (28), but also including Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan, are deemed to be involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

Nearly half of the newly listed entities, all based in China, were found to be supporting Chinese military modernization and sanctioned parties in Iran. Additionally, a significant number of Chinese and Pakistani entities were added for supporting ballistic missile and unsafeguarded nuclear activities, while several entities in Russia, Belarus, and one in Taiwan were cited for supporting Russia's military.

BIS also included a half-dozen entities for supporting human rights violations in China and Burma, largely through surveillance programs. Companies with cross-border dealings are advised to conduct frequent and updated counterparty screening to ensure compliance with these new restrictions.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Legal 500

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
